paras: The attempted lynching of Will Ingram took place in Eatonton, Putnam County, Georgia, on July 30 or 31, 1910, when a crowd pursued and fired at Ingram, a Black man accused of burglary, after he escaped from custody. Ingram survived after a white woman, Mrs. Susie Hillhouse, stood between him and the crowd, and he was returned to jail. Dispatches built around her intervention ran in papers from New York to Washington State and on the front page of the Black newspaper The Advocate.
Ingram, described in the reports as "a negro," had been arrested on an accusation of burglary and was held at Eatonton, where the Putnam County jail stood.

According to a dispatch printed in the New York Sun and other papers, Ingram broke away from the officer who had arrested him and fled through town, "pursued by a crowd firing at him." A second dispatch, carried in South Carolina papers, said instead that he had been foiled in an attempt "to set free all the prisoners in Putnam county jail," overpowered Deputy Sheriff Ingram Phillips, took the deputy's pistol, and broke through "a cordon of citizens." In that version he was hit by a bullet in the arm and fled with "several hundred persons behind him firing shotguns and pistols."

The chase ended in a residence section of the town, where Mrs. Susie Hillhouse, called "a prominent woman of this place," was leaving her home for church. The exhausted fugitive fell at her feet, begged her to save his life, and gave her his pistol, though the South Carolina dispatch said he threw it at her feet. Holding the weapon, she faced the crowd and, by the Sun's account, said it would be "a shame to lynch the negro" and that she would not allow "such an outrage on the law."

The crowd cheered her and promised that Ingram would not be harmed. Leaders of the mob then escorted him back to jail, with Mrs. Hillhouse going along to see that he was not hurt. The South Carolina version said only that she begged for his life "so effectually that he was returned to jail without further harm."
No report of charges against anyone in the crowd, of an inquiry into the shooting, or of Ingram's trial on the burglary charge appears in the coverage.

Most papers carried the story as a wire dispatch with Mrs. Hillhouse as its subject. On August 1 the New York Sun headlined it "Woman Foils a Mob" and the Newark Evening Star "White Woman Saves Negro"; the Barre Daily Times in Vermont ran "Woman Foils Lynchers" on August 2. The Yakima Herald in Washington printed the same text on August 3, and on August 4 the Greenville Journal in Ohio and the Owingsville Outlook in Kentucky ran a one-paragraph digest under "Saved by Woman's Bravery." In the Owingsville paper the item ran among briefs on a Black man killed by Sioux Falls officers and another killed by a posse near Mobile.

The South Carolina dispatch, which told the jail-break version, appeared in the Edgefield Advertiser and the Dillon Herald under "Surrendered to White Woman" and in the Bamberg Herald as "Woman Takes Negro." Both dispatches repeated the burglary accusation without qualification and named no one in the crowd that fired on Ingram.

The Advocate, a Black newspaper, ran the Hillhouse dispatch on its front page on August 4 under a stacked headline: "Georgia Woman Saves Negro, Accused of Burglary, from Mob Bent on His Death and Sees Him Safely Jailed." Its text, datelined July 31, printed the name as "Will Ongram," capitalized "Negro," left out Mrs. Hillhouse's remarks on lynching, and carried no comment of the paper's own.

The two dispatches differ on the date, the manner of escape and the wound. The South Carolina dispatch placed the escape on Saturday, July 30, while the Sun's July 31 dispatch said "to-day," a Sunday that fits Mrs. Hillhouse's leaving for church. Only the South Carolina dispatch reported a jail-break attempt, an attack on the deputy and a wound; the Hillhouse dispatch mentioned none of these. Estimates of the crowd ran from "more than a hundred" to "several hundred."

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Will Ingram
bases: A crowd described as a mob 'clamoring for the life' of Will Ingram chased and fired on him after his escape and was stopped from lynching him by a woman's intervention (A1, A2, A4).

A mob of more than a hundred or several hundred people sought to lynch Ingram, accused of burglary, and fired on him, but he survived and was returned to jail (A1, A2, A4); it was an attempted lynching, not a killing.

Two separately worded dispatches, the Hillhouse wire (A1, A2) and a South Carolina 'special' (A4, A7), agree that Ingram, accused of burglary, escaped, was chased and fired on by a crowd, and was saved by a white woman and returned to jail.

accounts.label: Hillhouse wire dispatch
accounts.gist: Ingram, accused of burglary, broke away from the officer and fled pursued by a crowd firing at him; Mrs. Hillhouse took his pistol, faced the mob, and the mob's leaders escorted him to jail.

accounts.label: South Carolina 'special' dispatch
accounts.gist: Ingram tried to free all prisoners in the Putnam County jail, overpowered Deputy Sheriff Ingram Phillips, took his pistol, was shot in the arm, and fled several hundred armed pursuers before surrendering to a white woman who begged for his life.

framing.detail: Northern papers ran the Hillhouse dispatch as a human-interest story, 'Woman Foils a Mob' and 'White Woman Saves Negro', quoting her that a lynching would be 'an outrage on the law'.
South Carolina papers ran a version stressing Ingram's alleged jail-break and attack on a deputy, headlined 'Surrendered to White Woman' and 'Woman Takes Negro'.
The Advocate put the Hillhouse dispatch on page 1 under 'Saves Negro, Accused of Burglary, from Mob Bent on His Death', capitalizing 'Negro', with no editorial comment.

conflicts.note: The Sunday date fits the detail that Mrs. Hillhouse was leaving for church; neither version is from a local paper.
